newsitem.title: ITALY: Zaire says refugees must go to Rwanda and Burundi.
newsitem.headline: Zaire says refugees must go to Rwanda and Burundi.

text.p: Zaire said on Thursday all aid for starving refugees in the east of the country should be sent to Rwanda and Burundi to encourage their return home and accused the world of "total indifference" to their fate.

As momentum built for a multinational intervention force to enter eastern Zaire, deputy prime minister Mutombo Bakafwa Nsenda said it was up to Rwanda and Burundi to take back the ethnic Hutu refugees at risk from fighting in the area.

"The fate of one million human beings is being played out amid the total indifference of the international community and of the governments of the places these people are from," Mutombo told a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit in Rome.

Instead of international understanding and recognition, Zaire had received "only indifference, ingratitude, even scorn" from Rwanda and Burundi, the United Nations and the international community, Mutombo said.

"That is why Zaire is launching a pressing appeal to the peoples of the world united on the occasion of this world summit on food security that all urgent action or all humanitarian aid destined for the refugees is delivered and distributed in their countries of origin, in Rwanda and Burundi and not in Zaire."
A member of the Burundi delegation at the summit, ambassador to Italy Jean-Baptiste Mbonyingingo, said his country was ready to accept back refugees to the best of its capacity.
"This is an accusation which is not justified," the envoy said when asked about Mutombo's charge that Burundi's Tutsi-dominated government had shunned its responsibility.

"To say it is up to others to take care of things is one thing, but the country (which receives the refugees) must also be concerned. It must act to encourage a peaceful return of the refugees," he told Reuters.
Mutombo's speech reflected Zaire's position since the start of the crisis but U.N. envoy Raymond Chretien said in Kinshasa on Wednesday that the stance had changed.
"They (Zaire and Rwanda) agreed...to help the Rwandan, Burundian or Zairean refugees on the ground on Zairean territory," Chretien said.
He added that both countries saw the role of a Canadian-led force, including U.S. troops, preparing for a mission to the area as to create the conditions for a voluntary return home of refugees.
Mutombo told Reuters that agreement had been given "on the condition that the force has a mission to evacuate...to maintain peace and help the refugees to return home".

"This is a condition which concerns the sovereignty of our country," he said. "Why should you do it (distribute aid) in Zaire, why? These refugees have a country...they have a government, why doesn't this government worry about its refugees."
He also expressed opposition to any dealings between aid agencies and Tutsi rebels who have seized Zaire's two eastern provinces bordering Rwanda in fighting since October 18.

"It is not in the interest of the refugees," Mutombo said when asked about efforts to bring aid to the city of Goma, where heavy fighting flared on Thursday between the rebels and their Hutu foes holed up in a teeming refugee camp.

Most of the refugees fled to Zaire from Rwanda in 1994 to escape a victorious Tutsi army which put an end to the killing by Hutus of some 800,000 Tutsis. They are now at risk from four weeks of fighting involving Tutsi rebels and Zairean troops.
The refugees, many of whom followed defeated Hutu soldiers out, fear reprisals if they go home. Hutu gunmen among them have intimidated any who tried to leave.
